review.review_reason: Internal Yaghan slavery remains researched-inconclusive while external/intergroup captivity is preserved directionally; no absence inference is made.

data.bounded_proposition: Slavery was an active, commodified household institution in the Khmer imperial capital/core immediately before 1300, independently attested by Zhou Daguan; earlier Angkorian epigraphy demonstrates deeper institutional continuity. data.required_abstention: Do not convert Zhou's household-number impressions into P-level/prevalence; do not universalize khñum as slave; do not assign modern ethnicity to Zhou's mountain/savage category; do not treat purchase origin as capture geography; do not color the whole empire from the capital.
data.evidence_locus: Angkor/Yasodharapura 1296-1297 as primary locus; earlier Angkorian temple/institutional inscription network as predecessor context
data.inference_extent: Exact-anchor capital/core household slavery supported; polity-wide uniformity, acquisition geography and prevalence unresolved.
data.law_practice_note: Exact-anchor evidence is observed household practice; earlier legal/epigraphic scholarship supplies institutional history but not one uniform 1300 slave code.
data.network_territorial_note: Household slave acquisition included people purchased from beyond the lowland core; origin, capture, sale and slaveholding locations remain separate and do not create source-territory practice claims.

data.geometry_unresolved_note: Angkor is a defensible near-anchor locus; the 1300 Khmer polity polygon requires separate historical geometry review and cannot inherit a uniform practice value from the capital.

review.review_reason: Zhou Daguan independently supports household slavery at Angkor in 1296-1297; polity-wide prevalence/extent remains withheld.
review.dependency_or_scope_note: Earlier Angkor epigraphy is predecessor context; shared angkor-personnel-corpus not counted as independent 1300 evidence.

Slavery existed in the connected coastal network, but current evidence does not establish slavery/enslavement at Great Zimbabwe or Great-Zimbabwe-specific slave-trade participation.
data.required_abstention: Do not infer forced/slave labor from monumentality, hierarchy, tribute or dependency; do not back-project later Mutapa/Torwa servants/slaves; do not transfer Kilwa/Sofala slavery to Great Zimbabwe; do not infer absence from collective labor.

data.inference_extent: Positive site-level political economy/labor context; slavery at site and target-specific slave-trade participation remain unresolved; no state-wide practice inference.
data.law_practice_note: No exact-anchor Great Zimbabwe written slave/status law recovered; archaeology and specialist political-economy reconstruction support labor organization/dependency but not a slave-status designation.
data.network_territorial_note: Great Zimbabwe participates in Indian Ocean commodity networks and connected Kilwa contains slavery near anchor, but connectivity does not establish Great Zimbabwe captive provenance or export.
data.historical_terms: communal work party; reciprocal labor; tribute; subject homestead; dependency; servants/slaves in later comparator; enslaved people at Kilwa

data.geometry_unresolved_note: Great Zimbabwe site may be a navigation locus after separate geometry review; no political-hinterland or slavery-practice polygon is authorized.

review.dependency_or_scope_note: No forced-labor inference from monumentality or trade connectivity.

data.bounded_proposition: Traditional/pre-contact Māori society included war-captive unfree statuses described through taurekareka/mōkai and commonly mapped to slavery/captivity. This applies to the social world surrounding the 1700 anchor, but exact distribution, prevalence, terminology and status rules across individual iwi/hapū remain unresolved.
data.required_abstention: Do not treat Māori as one 1700 polity; do not infer uniformity across iwi/hapū; do not map taurekareka/mōkai automatically to Atlantic chattel slavery; do not collapse dependent hapū/tribute into slave status; do not back-project Musket Wars scale/economics; do not infer every battle produced captives.
data.evidence_locus: Multiple traditional Māori community/source traditions; early-contact observations; later customary-law reconstruction across iwi/hapū contexts
data.inference_extent: Positive period/institution-level war-captive unfreedom; aggregate exact-1700 distribution and prevalence withheld.
data.law_practice_note: No single written Aotearoa-wide law; customary status reconstructed from oral tradition, early observers, ethnography and specialist synthesis. Institutional reality does not imply a uniform legal regime.
data.network_territorial_note: Captive movement can follow intergroup warfare, but no Aotearoa-wide slave-trade network or territorial prevalence is inferred.
data.historical_terms: taurekareka; mōkai; rangatira; tūtūā; tāngata; war captive; dependent hapū
data.category_mapping_note: Taurekareka is commonly rendered slave but the Waitangi Tribunal cautions that the translation is not entirely accurate; mōkai is broader/contextual; dependent tāngata/tribute relations remain separate.
data.language_access_limitations: English-language specialist/institutional syntheses and translated/edited early-contact sources reviewed; no exhaustive Māori-language oral-history corpus or iwi-by-iwi reconstruction; Scite cross-check unavailable due quota.
data.geometry_unresolved_note: Aotearoa or modern iwi boundaries cannot become a uniform 1700 practice polygon; any future geometry must be claim/member-locus specific.

review.review_reason: Traditional/pre-contact war-captive unfreedom is supported while exact 1700 cross-iwi/hapu distribution and category equivalence remain unresolved.
review.dependency_or_scope_note: No one Māori polity/regime; no Musket Wars back-projection.

The sacrificed people's slave status, wider Nobatian slaveholding prevalence and external slave-trade participation remain unresolved.

data.inference_extent: Positive royal-site coerced-death practice near anchor; slave status and polity-wide/external-trade extent withheld.
data.law_practice_note: No exact-anchor Nobatian legal/status corpus recovered; archaeology directly supports sacrificial practice but not juridical slave status.
data.network_territorial_note: Broader Middle Nile slavery/slave-taking is contextual; significant early external slave trade is not securely demonstrated and no Nobatia-500 trade network is assigned.
data.historical_terms: human sacrifice; retainer sacrifice; attendant/servant; slave; captive; slave-taking; external slave trade
data.category_mapping_note: Human retainer sacrifice is a secure practice category; older labels of sacrificed attendants as slaves are not adopted without independent status evidence.
data.language_access_limitations: English specialist archaeology/history and translated Procopius reviewed; no exhaustive Greek/Coptic/Old Nubian corpus; Scite cross-check unavailable due quota.
data.geometry_unresolved_note: Qustul/Ballana may serve as evidence loci after separate geometry review; no Nobatia-wide practice polygon is authorized.

review.review_reason: Royal human/retainer sacrifice near the anchor is supported while slave status, polity-wide slaveholding and external trade remain unresolved.
review.dependency_or_scope_note: Retainer sacrifice != slave status; later baqt not back-projected.

data.bounded_proposition: Around the 500 BCE horizon, a Qi-associated textual tradition preserves a redeemable personal-servitude relationship involving Yan Ying and Yue Shifu, but the current evidence does not securely locate that servitude within Qi territory or date it to the exact anchor. Qi territorial slavery/servitude at 500 BCE remains researched-inconclusive.
data.required_abstention: Do not relocate the Zhongmou episode into Qi; do not treat the received narrative as an exact-year administrative record; do not count Yanzi chunqiu, Lüshi chunqiu and Shiji parallels as independent attestations; do not map 臣僕/僕/贖/鬻 automatically to hereditary chattel slavery; do not back-project Qin/Han law; do not infer prevalence, trade scale or a practice polygon.
data.evidence_locus: Zhongmou in the Yue Shifu narrative; Yanzi chunqiu textual tradition associated with Yan Ying/Qi; later dependent parallels; broad Eastern Zhou slavery/status synthesis
data.inference_extent: Positive near-anchor contextual evidence for redeemable personal servitude/dependency; exact Qi territorial occurrence, legal classification, institutionalization and prevalence withheld.
data.law_practice_note: No exact-anchor Qi legal/status text was recovered; narrative vocabulary supports a bounded servitude relation but not a Qi legal regime, heritability rule or prevalence claim.
data.network_territorial_note: The servitude episode occurs at Zhongmou during a journey to Jin; Yan Ying's Qi identity does not convert it into territorial Qi practice, and no Qi-specific slave-trade network is assigned.
data.historical_terms: 臣僕; 僕; 贖; 鬻; 縲絏
data.category_mapping_note: The story supports a redeemable servant/dependency status. Exact juridical mapping to later 奴婢 or modern chattel/property slavery is unresolved.
data.language_access_limitations: Received Chinese text checked via Chinese Text Project plus English specialist textual scholarship; no exhaustive excavated-manuscript/paleographic or Chinese-language historiographical survey.
data.geometry_unresolved_note: Qi polity identity is valid at the anchor, but no subject-evidence locus supports a Qi-wide practice polygon; Zhongmou is not silently attached to Qi.

review.review_reason: The complete packet correctly leaves Qi territorial slavery/servitude researched-inconclusive while preserving the Yue Shifu narrative only as near-anchor contextual evidence. The Zhongmou locus, composite transmission, category uncertainty and exact-anchor limits are explicit.
review.dependency_or_scope_note: Acceptance validates the bounded inconclusive evidence state, not a positive Qi slavery claim. Three Yue Shifu textual witnesses remain one narrative family.

data.bounded_proposition: Around 1400 the Swahili maritime network participated in a persistent but comparatively modest medieval slave trade, with concrete node-level slavery evidence at Kilwa and bounded fifteenth-century archaeological evidence at Songo Mnara. Network participation is supported; coast-wide territorial practice, uniformity and scale remain unresolved.
data.required_abstention: Do not infer one Swahili polity or uniform coast-wide practice; do not infer slave trading from maritime connectivity alone; do not generalize Kilwa or Songo Mnara to every node; do not project nineteenth-century Zanzibar plantation scale backward; do not convert source counts into prevalence or trade volume.
data.evidence_locus: Kilwa 1331; Rasulid/Yemeni maritime-customs context for thirteenth/fourteenth-century East Africa-Arabia trade; Songo Mnara fifteenth century; Tumbatu/Mkokotoni c.1000-1400; specialist Swahili-coast synthesis
data.inference_extent: Positive network-level slave-trade participation around the anchor plus bounded node-level local slavery/practice; territorial prevalence, participation by every port and exact network volume withheld.
data.law_practice_note: No single coast-wide legal regime is assigned; Islamic legal/social context is relevant but not used to infer uniform local law. Practice and network participation rest on bounded primary/site evidence plus specialist synthesis.
data.network_territorial_note: External/network slave-trade participation is supported. Local territorial slavery is supported only at bounded nodes; network membership does not transfer territorial practice to all ports or coastlands.
data.historical_terms: slave; enslaved person; captive; raid; client; dependent; domestic worker; migrant; maritime trade
data.category_mapping_note: Slave trading, local slaveholding, raiding, clientship, migration and other dependency remain distinct; archaeological low-status proxies are not automatic slave-status proof.
data.language_access_limitations: English specialist scholarship and translated Ibn Battuta reviewed; no exhaustive Arabic, Portuguese, Swahili or Rasulid archival corpus and no source-native customs edition reconstructed in this pass.
data.geometry_unresolved_note: No route line or Swahili-coast polygon is promoted to slavery-practice geometry; Kilwa, Songo Mnara and Tumbatu/Mkokotoni remain bounded evidence/navigation loci.

review.review_reason: Multiple evidence types support medieval network participation in slave trading around the anchor while the packet keeps node-specific local slavery, network participation, coast-wide territorial practice and trade scale separate.
review.dependency_or_scope_note: Network-positive only. Kilwa/Songo Mnara do not generalize to every Swahili node; later Zanzibar plantation scale is excluded.

data.bounded_proposition: Ifugao communities at 1700 remain researched-inconclusive for slavery or a specific servile institution. Later ethnographic evidence supports child sale, debt bondage, captivity and slaveholding in some Ifugao communities, but its temporal reach back to 1700 and exact category mapping are unresolved.
data.required_abstention: Do not infer exact-1700 slavery from early-20th-century ethnography; do not infer slavery from archaeological hierarchy/status differentiation; do not collapse himbut, debt peon, servant, captive and slave into one category; do not generalize Tuwali/Old Kiyyangan or later ethnography to every Ifugao community.
data.evidence_locus: Old Kiyyangan and wider Ifugao archaeological landscape c.1600-1800; Barton early-20th-century ethnography; later comparative Cordillera class-structure scholarship
data.inference_extent: Exact-period social transformation is supported, but exact-1700 slavery/status practice is unresolved; later traditional unfreedom is positive contextual evidence only.
data.law_practice_note: No exact-1700 written Ifugao legal corpus recovered. Later customary-law ethnography records coercive status/property relations but does not securely date them to 1700.
data.network_territorial_note: No external slave-trade network is assigned at 1700. Later Barton material includes movement/sale toward Nueva Vizcaya and Isabela, but this is not projected backward or generalized region-wide.
data.historical_terms: himbut; child sale; debt bondage; captive; servant; slave; nawatwat/debt-peon terminology in later comparative analysis
data.category_mapping_note: Barton uses slavery language for himbut and related practices; Scott's later comparison cautions that Ifugao dependency/propertylessness should not be mechanically equated with a chattel-slave class. Source-native terms and disagreement are preserved.
data.language_access_limitations: English-language colonial-era ethnography and modern archaeology reviewed; no exact-1700 indigenous written source or exhaustive Ifugao-language oral-history/genealogical corpus reconstructed.
data.geometry_unresolved_note: Old Kiyyangan may serve as a local evidence/navigation locus; no Ifugao-wide slavery-practice polygon is authorized.

review.review_reason: The packet does not project Barton’s later traditional ethnography into 1700. It records exact-anchor slavery/status as researched-inconclusive while preserving independently supported seventeenth/eighteenth-century social context and later child-sale/debt-bondage/slaveholding evidence.
review.dependency_or_scope_note: Acceptance validates the exact-anchor inconclusive result. Barton 1919/1922 remain one evidence family; IAP archaeology does not become slave-status proof.

data.bounded_proposition: The Khanate of Kokand participated in slavery and captive enslavement in the early nineteenth century, but the evidence recovered does not securely date a specific slaveholding, slave-trading or enslavement event to the exact 1800 anchor. Exact-1800 Kokand practice remains researched-inconclusive.
data.required_abstention: Do not transfer Bukhara/Khiva slave systems to Kokand; do not project 1820s captive enslavement or later nineteenth-century slaveholding backward to 1800; do not equate prisoners or conscripts with slaves; do not use the later territorial maximum; do not infer prevalence or a practice polygon.

data.inference_extent: Broader-period Kokand slavery/captive enslavement is supported, but verified target-specific evidence recovered is later than 1800; exact-anchor territorial occurrence and institution withheld.
data.law_practice_note: No exact-1800 Kokand slave-sale, manumission, court or legal record recovered. General Hanafi slave law and regional practice are context, not exact-anchor proof.
data.network_territorial_note: Later evidence supports captive enslavement and transfer of enslaved Chinese persons in Kokand's political/frontier network; Bukhara/Khiva systems are excluded as territorial substitutes.
data.historical_terms: qul; ghulam; captive; prisoner; conscript; slave; manumission
data.category_mapping_note: Central Asian qul/ghulam categories are recognized specialist slavery terms, but prisoner/conscript and later Ghalcha/Pamiri military status are not automatically mapped to slave status without source-specific evidence.
data.language_access_limitations: English specialist scholarship and an English 1834 report reviewed; no exhaustive Persian, Chagatai, Uzbek, Russian or Kokand legal/archival corpus.
data.geometry_unresolved_note: The early Fergana-centered polity frame is retained; later expansion is excluded and no slavery-practice polygon is authorized.

review.review_reason: The packet explicitly refuses to back-project 1820s/1830s Kokand captive enslavement into 1800 and excludes Bukhara/Khiva as territorial substitutes. The broader-period positive and small-scale specialist context are retained without exact-anchor promotion.
review.dependency_or_scope_note: Acceptance validates the exact-1800 inconclusive state, not an exact-anchor positive. Prisoner/conscript status and later territorial expansion remain non-inferred.
